community.name: The Commons
community.description: Where people at Riverbend ask the questions that do not fit anywhere else. Anyone can post; be specific and be kind.

discussions.title: Where exactly is the line on escalating a refund?
discussions.label: question
discussions.author: student-04
discussions.content:
The course says escalate above the threshold, and I know where to find the number. What I cannot work out is the case where a customer asks for two smaller refunds in the same week that add up to more than it.

Do I treat them separately, or together? Splitting to stay underneath is explicitly not allowed when we do it, so I assume the same applies when it happens by accident.

comments.author: student-11
comments.content: Together. The rule is about the total exposure on the account, not the shape of the requests. I raise anything that crosses the line cumulatively within a month and nobody has ever minded.

comments.author: student-02
comments.content: Worth adding a note on the account when you do, so whoever picks it up next can see why it was escalated rather than working it out from the amounts.

discussions.title: The running confusion list actually works
discussions.label: showcase
discussions.author: student-17
discussions.content:
Sceptical about this one at first, but I kept the list through my first fortnight and it turned into the most useful thing I have written here.

Half of it answered itself by week three. The other half became four questions for my manager that we would otherwise never have got to, and two of them turned out to be gaps in the handbook rather than gaps in me.

comments.author: student-23
comments.content: Same. The bit nobody says is that the list stops being possible after about six weeks; you stop noticing what is strange.

discussions.title: How do you phrase a substitute without overselling it?
discussions.label: question
discussions.author: student-08
discussions.content:
When the line they want is unavailable I always feel like I am either underselling the alternative or glossing over the difference. Both end badly: one loses the sale, the other comes back as a return.

What wording do people use?

comments.author: student-31
comments.content: I say what it is for first, then name the difference before the similarity: "This one is the same spec but the lead time is three weeks rather than one. Does that still work for the job?" Putting the drawback first means they trust the rest of it.

comments.author: student-15
comments.content: And if there genuinely is not a good substitute, saying so outright has never once lost me an account. Pushing a bad one has.

discussions.title: Reminder: check whether the metric definition moved
discussions.label: idea
discussions.author: student-29
discussions.content:
We spent most of a meeting last month explaining a jump that turned out to be a definition change: returns started being counted when processed rather than when requested.

Suggestion: whoever changes a definition adds a line to the report footer with the date. Costs nothing, saves an afternoon.

comments.author: student-06
comments.content: Strongly in favour. Would also catch the case where the person who changed it has left.

discussions.title: Welcome: how this space works
discussions.label: announcement
discussions.author: student-00
discussions.content:
This is the place for questions that do not have an obvious owner, and for writing up something you worked out the hard way so the next person does not have to.

Two norms: be specific enough that someone can actually answer, and answer in the open rather than by direct message. The second one is what makes the first one worth doing.
